preamble: Retraction of [s] to the retroflex [ʂ]. In Sanskrit the dental s becomes the lingual (retroflex) ṣ after any vowel other than a/ā and after k and r, unless it is word-final or followed by r; this ruki rule is a live sandhi process, so a root-initial s turns into ṣ after prefixes in i or u (prati + sthā > pratiṣṭhā́). Sanskrit s also assimilates to ṣ before a retroflex stop ṭ across word boundaries. In Russian, /s/ assimilates in place to a following retroflex /ʂ/, so с + шить is pronounced [ʂːɨtʲ].

examples.note: Root-initial s becomes ṣ after the i of the prefix (Whitney §185a); the following t becomes ṭ
Same rule after the prefix ni- (Whitney §185a)
Final s becomes ṣ before an initial lingual stop ṭ in external sandhi (Whitney §170c)
Prefix-final /s/ assimilates to the following /ʂ/; careful speech keeps [sʂɨtʲ]

context: Sanskrit: s after vowels other than a/ā and after k, r, and before ṭ; Russian: /s/ before /ʂ/
